'Links to other factors' live in edges.json (single source of truth for the graph) -- the Network/Scenario views resolve a factor's links from there. currentSituation cells marked provenance:'notes-empty' were blank in the PDF; 'added' cells were filled via web search (see source+date). Every numeric example is transcribed verbatim from research.pdf, not summarised.

factors.name: Labour Market and Incomes
factors.segmentsHitRaw: Homebuilding (affordability); Residential Rental (rent-to-income); Retail (spending power); Office (white-collar jobs); Hotels (discretionary travel)
factors.whyItMatters: Rents and mortgages are paid from people's income. Without income growth, higher rents and prices have nothing to stand on.

direction.up: Rising real wages + low unemployment. Employment growing + pay rising faster than inflation (positive real wages).
direction.down: Rising unemployment + very strong jobs data can HURT (keeps central banks from cutting).

factors.backdrop: Recession with layoffs (rising unemployment). Very bad combination: tight labour plus sticky inflation.
factors.example: REAL WAGES MUST BE RISING: A family earns 100 and buys a home for 100. Five years later the home costs 150 but the family earns only 120. They now need a much bigger share of pay to own the same home, so fewer families can buy.

watchouts.title: #1 AFFORDABILITY
watchouts.detail: Depends on three things: Home Price, Mortgage Rate, Household Income. Common test: housing costs above 30% of income is unaffordable. Report says prices would need to fall about 38% for homes to be cheaper than renting now, at mortgage rates of 6.7%.

watchouts.title: #2 LABOUR TRENDS
watchouts.detail: Office follows white-collar jobs. Logistics follows consumer spending and goods trade. Retail follows real disposable income. Hotels follow discretionary spending, the first thing cut when jobs get uncertain.

watchouts.title: #3 GOOD-NEWS-IS-BAD-NEWS
watchouts.detail: Strong jobs -> strong wages -> sticky inflation -> central bank cuts slower.

indicators.sources: FRED and BLS (US); Eurostat and the ECB wage tracker (Europe); Passport for household income by country.

scenarios.whatHappens: More households can pay rent and mortgages; firms need more space
scenarios.hurt: Rate-sensitive REITs, if strong jobs keep inflation sticky and delay cuts
scenarios.netRead: Good for demand, bad for timing if cuts get delayed

scenarios.whatHappens: Fewer buyers and tenants; more missed payments; empty desks
scenarios.helped: Rate cuts eventually, since a weak economy lowers rates
scenarios.hurt: Office, hotels, retail, rental in the affected city, homebuilders
scenarios.netRead: Cuts come, but demand weakens first, so bearish near term

scenarios.whatHappens: Affordability improves without prices having to fall; rents are easier to pay
scenarios.hurt: Possibly rates, if wage growth feeds inflation
scenarios.netRead: Best when inflation is also falling

scenarios.whatHappens: Housing takes a bigger share of pay; more arrears; people double up
scenarios.helped: Cheaper housing and renting over buying
scenarios.hurt: Homebuilding, rental collections, retail, entry-level homes
scenarios.netRead: Bearish, even if rates fall

factors.additionalNotes: Important (p.8): renting is cheaper than buying once the mortgage/rent ratio goes above 1.0. Page 8 also mentions a graph that isn't actually there.

USA.situation: 4.2% in September 2026, up from 4.1% in August -- rising rather than falling.
USA.source: US BLS, Employment Situation Summary, Sept 2026 (bls.gov/news.release/empsit.nr0.htm)

USA.situation: Only 29,000 new jobs added in September 2026 -- well below expectations. Wage growth is slowing too. A cooling job market, but not a sharp downturn.

EU.situation: 6.4% in August 2026 (euro area, seasonally adjusted), holding at that level since February 2026 -- stable, not deteriorating.

The economy is actually doing well: a business activity index (PMI) hit a 41-month high in September 2026. Combined with inflation picking back up (see the Inflation factor), that's exactly the 'good news keeps the ECB from cutting rates' problem described in watch-out #3 below.
EU.source: S&P Global Eurozone Composite PMI, Sept 2026

factors.name: Consumer Confidence and Savings
factors.segmentsHitRaw: Homebuilding (first to feel it); Residential Rental (renters who delay buying stay renters); Home Improvement Retail and Building Products (renovation spending)
factors.whyItMatters: Home is the biggest purchase most people make. They commit only when they trust the job and economic situation. Confidence also drives spending on furniture, renovations, and moving.

direction.up: Rising confidence + rebuilding savings rate. Lower expected inflation.

factors.backdrop: Inflation, job worries or geopolitical shocks make households pessimistic.
factors.example: A couple is ready to buy. News says layoffs are coming and prices are falling. They decide to wait six months. Multiply by a million couples and home sales drop even though nobody lost a job yet.

watchouts.title: #1 CONFIDENCE LEADS, SALES FOLLOW
watchouts.detail: Confidence is always the early warning. If confidence rises while sales are still flat, the recovery may be starting.

watchouts.title: #2 SAVINGS-DEPOSIT PROBLEM
watchouts.detail: A buyer usually needs a deposit before buying a house (e.g. 20% down). A savings rate of ~3% means most households are saving very little. Even if they could afford the monthly payment, they cannot clear the upfront cash. This is why builders are offering more mortgage-rate buy-downs: 66% of builders offered incentives in September and 38% cut base prices.

watchouts.title: #3 FEEDBACK LOOP
watchouts.detail: Falling prices make people expect further falls, so they wait. Waiting lowers sales, pushing prices down more, repeating. Can also run upward. This is why changing mood can move housing markets more than numbers -- markets overshoot both ways.

indicators.sources: University of Michigan, BEA, NAHB (US); European Commission and GfK (Europe).

scenarios.whatHappens: Buyers return; builders order land and start homes; sales and renovation spending rise
scenarios.helped: Homebuilding, existing-home sales, home retail, building products
scenarios.hurt: Nobody directly; the risk is inventory flooding in as sellers list
scenarios.netRead: Bullish, especially if it arrives before supply floods the market

scenarios.whatHappens: Buyers wait; builders cut starts and offer incentives; margins fall
scenarios.hurt: Homebuilding, retail, building products, existing sales
scenarios.netRead: Bearish; rate cuts may not bring buyers back quickly

scenarios.whatHappens: More deposits and bigger buffers; fewer defaults when shocks hit
scenarios.hurt: Retail and spending in the short run, as people save instead
scenarios.netRead: Bullish for entry demand and credit quality

scenarios.whatHappens: Fewer deposits, thin buffers, more missed payments after shocks
scenarios.hurt: Entry-level homebuilding, rental collections, first-time buyers
scenarios.netRead: Bearish; the report shows about 3% saving against 7.3% in 2019

USA.situation: The savings rate right now in the US is about 3%, against 7.3% in 2019. Households lack down payments.
Sentiment is weak because of inflation and geopolitics. People don't buy homes when they feel insecure, so confidence leads transactions.

EU.situation: Headline HICP inflation accelerated to 3.8% in September 2026 (highest since Sept 2023), with core (ex-energy/food) inflation at 2.5% -- both rising for a third straight month, squeezing real incomes just as the ECB is holding rates at 2.50%.
6.4% (Aug 2026), stable since February -- see Labour factor for the full picture.

A French government bond sell-off (10y OAT above 5% for the first time since 2002, amid a budget standoff and protests) is the clearest confidence/geopolitical risk in the data right now -- see Rates factor.

factors.name: Inflation and Energy Prices
factors.segmentsHitRaw: The notes just say 'ALL OF THEM' with no detail. We listed every segment here, since energy costs, construction costs, and interest-rate expectations really do touch the whole real estate chain -- this makes that claim specific instead of vague.
factors.whyItMatters: Rewritten by us -- the notes here were a word-for-word copy of the Consumer Confidence section. Energy is a direct cost for running buildings (heating, cooling, power), for construction (fuel, materials like cement and steel), and for household budgets (competing with rent). Inflation more broadly: (1) drives how fast the central bank cuts or raises rates, (2) determines whether rents with built-in inflation increases actually keep up with real costs, and (3) explains the 'brown discount' -- older, energy-wasteful buildings sell for less as energy costs and efficiency rules bite (this connects to the Policy factor's energy-rules section).

direction.up: Energy prices rising; running and building costs climb; household budgets shrink; inflation rises.
direction.down: Energy prices falling; lower running costs and materials costs; household spending power rises.

factors.backdrop: Our own addition, since the notes didn't have one for this factor: supply shocks (energy, commodities), a tight labour market pushing wages and prices up together, or an overheating economy.
factors.example: Our own example, since the notes didn't have one for this factor: say energy costs for running an office building jump 30%. An old, inefficient building with no inflation-linked lease absorbs that cost directly, cutting its profit. A newer, efficient building with a green lease passes more of the cost to tenants. That gap in outcomes is the 'brown discount' in practice.

watchouts.title: Correction flagged, not silently fixed
watchouts.detail: The thesis opener says 'Rates should be decreasing... Europe is experiencing deflation.' The line directly beneath it, sourced to Eurostat, says the opposite: 'inflation excluding energy is substantially lower than headline inflation, but Europe is not currently experiencing broad-based deflation.' Treat the Eurostat-sourced line as correct.

indicators.sources: BLS and Fed (US); Eurostat and ECB (Europe).

scenarios.helped: Listed REITs, homebuilders, buyers, leveraged owners
scenarios.hurt: Owners relying on inflation-linked rent rises (slower rent growth)

scenarios.helped: Owners with indexed leases (towers, some logistics); hard-asset owners
scenarios.hurt: REITs with fixed leases, builders, buyers, leveraged developers
scenarios.netRead: Bearish for timing; cuts get pushed out

scenarios.helped: Older buildings, cement/glass/brick users, households, Europe especially
scenarios.hurt: Little direct harm; less urgency to retrofit
scenarios.netRead: Bullish, and quiet but powerful for Europe

scenarios.helped: Efficient new buildings (they cost less to run)
scenarios.hurt: Older office and flats, builders, materials users, Europe more than US
scenarios.netRead: Bearish; this is the current risk in the report

USA.situation: A cooling job market (unemployment up to 4.2%, weak hiring) is the main signal pointing toward rate cuts -- see the Labour factor for detail. We didn't independently verify the latest CPI number.

EU.situation: 3.8% in September 2026 -- accelerated for a third consecutive month, the highest since September 2023 (up from 3.2% in August).
2.5% in September 2026, up from 2.4%. Also rising, though still well below the headline number. This is the Eurostat fact that corrects the notes' deflation claim.

The ECB raised its deposit rate from 2.00% to 2.50% over the year to October 2026 -- i.e. rates have been rising, not falling, as inflation re-accelerated alongside resilient growth (composite PMI at a 41-month high). This is the opposite of the thesis's base case and is the single most important real-world update to flag.

factors.name: Demographics and Household Formation
factors.segmentsHitRaw: Residential rental (young and mobile households); Homebuilding (first-time buyers); Senior housing and healthcare (ageing); Student housing; Manufactured-home communities (retirees)
factors.whyItMatters: Every new household needs a home to rent or buy. Population growth, age mix, household size and migration decide how much housing is needed over years. This sets the trend and is SLOW.

direction.up: More households + a large young cohort entering their buying years (working years).
direction.down: Shrinking or ageing population hurts demand -- UNLESS household size is also falling (more homes needed per person).

factors.backdrop: When the large age group reaches the household-forming stage of life (mid-20s to 40s), this turns into purchases only when jobs and affordability allow -- otherwise young adults stay with parents or rent.
factors.example: A wave of people born in the same years turns 30. Many leave their parents' homes and look for a flat. If they cannot afford to buy, they rent, so rental demand rises first and buying demand shows up later.

watchouts.title: #1 HOUSEHOLDS, NOT PEOPLE
watchouts.detail: Japan is one of the clearest real-world examples of how demographic decline affects real estate -- but with a twist: Japan's population is shrinking while its number of households has continued to increase.

indicators.sources: US Census Bureau, NAR (US); Eurostat, national statistics offices, Passport (Europe).

scenarios.scenario: Household formation rises (young adults move out, immigration up)
scenarios.whatHappens: More homes needed; rents and sales demand rise
scenarios.helped: Rental, homebuilding, building products, home retail
scenarios.hurt: Nobody directly; the risk is supply not keeping up and prices rising out of reach
scenarios.netRead: Bullish if supply and jobs allow it

scenarios.whatHappens: Fewer homes needed; vacancy rises
scenarios.hurt: Rental, homebuilding, local retail, shrinking regions

scenarios.hurt: Single-family and apartment landlords
scenarios.netRead: Good for builders, mixed for rental REITs

scenarios.hurt: Homebuilders, home retail, building products

EU.situation: Just under 452 million as of 1 January 2026.
Not found as a specific current figure in this research pass -- flagged as a genuine gap rather than estimated.

factors.name: Construction Costs, Materials and Labour
factors.segmentsHitRaw: Homebuilding (margins); Building products; Wood and lumber; Developers and development REITs; Logistics and multifamily developers; Home improvement retail
factors.whyItMatters: Costs set the price at which new property makes sense to build. High costs reduce new supply, which can support values of existing buildings. They also squeeze builder margins and push new homes out of reach for buyers. This is why it matters that if costs increase, builders with a big backlog of buildings or large portfolio are better insulated.

direction.down: Sharp rises hurt builders -- BUT are good for owners of existing buildings (new competition gets harder to build).

factors.backdrop: Strong construction demand and supply-chain disruption push costs up (2020-22). Tariffs, energy shocks and labour shortages can do the same. Cost falls come after demand cools or supply chains clear.
factors.example: A builder spends 80 to build a home and sells it for 100. If costs rise to 90 and buyers will not pay more than 100, profit drops from 20 to 10. The builder may stop building, so fewer homes arrive next year.

watchouts.title: #1 SCALE WINS IN A SQUEEZE
watchouts.detail: Public homebuilders (35-40% of the market) can absorb lower prices better than small builders because of scale and lower cost of capital. When costs rise, big builders squeeze suppliers and take share from small ones.

watchouts.title: #2 VOLATILE MATERIALS, STICKY LABOUR
watchouts.detail: Lumber can swing sixfold in a year, then collapse 70%. Labour costs rise slowly and do not fall. Materials make the cycle's spikes, while labour creates a steady rise that never reverses. Builders lock in suppliers and prefer to buy land with options rather than own it -- Lennar holds 98% of its lots through options or joint ventures.

watchouts.title: #3 DEVELOPMENT SPREAD
watchouts.detail: A developer builds only when the yield on cost (net income from the new building divided by what it cost to build) is clearly higher than the market cap rate (the yield buyers pay for a finished building). If costs and rates both rise, the spread vanishes and no one builds -- bearish for new supply, bullish for existing assets later.

indicators.sources: BLS and NAHB (US); Eurostat construction cost indices, national statistics, Passport (Europe).

scenarios.whatHappens: Builders' margins widen; new homes get cheaper
scenarios.hurt: Materials makers (lower prices); existing owners (more new supply later)
scenarios.netRead: Good for builders, mixed for lumber and materials names

scenarios.whatHappens: Margins squeeze; builders cut starts or raise prices

USA.situation: Construction cost inflation has been low single digit in 2024-25. Over 90% of the value of residential construction goods is made domestically.
Builder gross margin fell from about 27% in 2022 to 20.3% in Q3 2026, and operating margin from about 20% to about 11%.

EU.situation: Building costs in the EU rose 1.7% in Q2 2026 alone, and the pace is picking up -- the opposite of the US trend above. Total rise since 2015: 48.2%.

factors.name: Housing Supply and the Existing-Home Lock-in
factors.segmentsHitRaw: Existing-home market (new-home inventory); Homebuilding; Residential rental and multifamily developers (vacancy and absorption); Manufactured-home communities
factors.whyItMatters: Supply against demand sets prices, rents and vacancy. Too little supply pushes values up. Too much pushes values down and forces discounts. It is the balance, not the level, that matters.

direction.up: Balanced market (about 4-6 months of supply, vacancy near average).
direction.down: Too much inventory hurts prices and builders. Too little hurts transactions and keeps prices high.

factors.backdrop: After a building boom or demand drop, supply outruns demand. The lock-in effect applies when many owners hold cheap old mortgages and rates are much higher today; it fades as time passes or as rates fall.
factors.example: A town has 100 homes for sale and 100 buyers a month, so supply lasts one month and prices rise. If sales halve to 50 buyers a month, the same 100 homes last two months and sellers start cutting prices.

watchouts.title: LOCK-IN EFFECT (mechanism)
watchouts.detail: You bought a house in 2021 with a 2% fixed mortgage. Today, new mortgages cost 6%. You want to move to a bigger house, but doing so means giving up your cheap 2% mortgage and taking out a new loan at 6%. So you decide not to sell. Millions of homeowners making the same decision creates the lock-in effect.

watchouts.title: #1 SELLERS OUTNUMBER BUYERS SHIFT
watchouts.detail: Sellers now outnumber buyers by the most in a decade -- a buyer's market. This often precedes falling prices. Morningstar expects existing-home prices to come under additional pressure in 2027 as inventory normalises.

watchouts.title: #2 RENTAL SUPPLY WAVE
watchouts.detail: Multifamily construction surged in 2021-22 when rents were rising and cap rates were low. Those buildings are now completing. Rental vacancy has climbed from 5.6% to 7.3% and absorption has slowed. Morningstar is cautious on multifamily in 2027.

watchouts.title: #3 RATE CUTS HELP VOLUMES BEFORE PRICES
watchouts.detail: Rates fall -> lock-in loosens -> more owners list -> supply rises -> prices may not rise much even with cheaper mortgages.

indicators.sources: US Census Bureau, NAR, FHFA (US); Eurostat, national agencies, local brokers (Europe).

EU.situation: Much smaller in Europe than in the US. Most European mortgages are variable-rate or fixed for only 5-10 years, unlike the US's typical 30-year fixed rate -- so far fewer European owners are stuck holding onto an old cheap rate.

factors.name: Government Policy and Regulation
factors.segmentsHitRaw: Residential rental (rent control); Homebuilding and developers (zoning, permits, impact fees); Office and retail (energy-efficiency rules); REITs (tax regimes); Building products (tariffs and subsidies)
factors.whyItMatters: Zoning and permitting cap supply. Rent rules cap income. Energy rules force spending on buildings. Taxes and subsidies change the cost of owning. Policy is slow to change but, once it does, it resets returns for years.

direction.up: Pro-supply reform helps builders and renters but can cap existing-owner gains. Tax relief and subsidies help demand.
direction.down: Rent caps and tough energy rules hurt landlord returns.

factors.backdrop: Policy usually changes after a political reaction to a visible problem: unaffordable rents, housing shortages, climate targets or high energy bills. Expect the strongest reaction after rents or prices have risen sharply.
factors.example: A city freezes rents for three years. Tenants are happy, but landlords can no longer pass on higher costs, so they stop maintaining, sell, or convert flats to offices or hotels. Fewer rental homes are built in the next cycle.

watchouts.title: #1 ZONING AND SUPPLY (the notes misspell this "zooming")
watchouts.detail: Zoning decides what can be built where. Strict rules and slow permits mean less gets built, keeping prices high. Loosening those rules builds more supply, but only after a long delay. That helps builders and renters, but can slow price growth for people who already own homes.

watchouts.title: #2 RENT CONTROL
watchouts.detail: Caps on rent increases protect tenants but reduce landlord income and returns. Investors then price in lower growth and may avoid regulated markets. Over time, supply of rental homes falls. Look at whether new buildings are exempt, whether caps are indexed to inflation, and how often rules change.

watchouts.title: #3 ENERGY AND CLIMATE RULES
watchouts.detail: Buildings are a large source of emissions. Rules requiring better energy ratings push owners to spend capital on insulation and heating systems. Owners of older, poorly rated offices and homes face the biggest costs, and those assets may trade at a discount (a 'brown discount'). Owners of efficient buildings can gain. Links to energy prices (Inflation factor).

indicators.sources: Government and legislative trackers, EU Commission, national housing ministries, law-firm briefings.

EU.situation: New buildings must produce zero emissions by 2030 (2028 for public buildings). For existing homes, countries must upgrade the worst-performing 16% by 2030, and the worst 26% by 2033. This is the rule behind the 'brown discount' in watch-out #3 below.

Germany caps rent increases in tight housing markets (the Mietpreisbremse). France caps rents in Paris, Lille, and other specific cities. Rules differ a lot by country and even by city -- there's no single EU-wide rent policy.
EU.source: General regulatory knowledge, not independently re-verified against a live source this pass

factors.name: Credit Conditions and Bank Lending
factors.segmentsHitRaw: Commercial real estate (office most, because lenders avoid it); Developers and construction (construction loans); Leveraged REITs; Multifamily buyers; Homebuyers (mortgage approval and spreads)
factors.whyItMatters: Property is bought and built with borrowed money. The policy rate sets the base cost, but lenders also decide how much to lend (LTV), at what spread, and whether to refinance at all. Credit can tighten even when rates fall.

direction.up: Easy credit (low spreads, high LTV, many lenders) helps prices and volumes.
direction.down: Tight credit (higher spreads, lower LTV, fewer lenders) hurts, and can trigger forced sales. Both effects arrive faster than demographic or supply changes.

factors.ltvDefinitionFlag: The notes define LTV (loan-to-value) as Debt divided by Enterprise Value. The usual definition is Debt divided by Property Value -- for REITs, often Net Debt divided by Gross Asset Value.
factors.backdrop: After losses, a rate shock or a recession. A refinancing wall (many loans maturing at once) at much higher rates makes the problem worse. Credit loosens when spreads fall, banks regain confidence and rates drop.
factors.example: A landlord borrowed 70% of a building's value at 3%. The loan matures, rates are 6% and the bank now lends only 55%. The landlord must find the missing cash or sell, even though the building is the same.

watchouts.title: #1 LENDER'S LEVERS
watchouts.detail: Lenders decide (1) the rate or spread, (2) the loan-to-value (LTV) and (3) the minimum coverage, such as DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) and debt yield. When rates rise, DSCR falls even if the building is unchanged, so lenders cut the loan size -- a refinancing can require fresh equity even when the property performs well.

watchouts.title: #2 BANK VS MARKET FUNDING
watchouts.detail: Banks lend on their balance sheet and tighten quickly after losses. Capital markets (bonds, CMBS) reopen when spreads tighten. The US uses markets more, so it recovers faster. Europe's bank-led system reacts more slowly but with less volatility. Private credit funds now compete with banks, at higher prices.

watchouts.title: #3 SIGNALS OF STRESS
watchouts.detail: Rising delinquencies, falling loan origination, wider spreads on real estate bonds, more special servicing in CMBS, lender surveys showing tighter standards, and growing distressed sales. For credit investors, these show up in bond prices before they show up in property prices.

indicators.note: 'Indicators to watch' field header exists in the notes but is empty for this factor.

USA.situation: Median FOMC projection points to further easing toward 4.1% by end-2026 as the labour market cools -- directionally supportive for credit conditions.

EU.situation: Banks got a bit more cautious: 9% tightened standards for home loans, 7% for business loans, 12% for consumer credit. They expect to keep tightening a little into Q3 2026, mainly because they're worried about the economy, not because funding itself got more expensive.
EU.source: ECB euro area Bank Lending Survey

factors.name: GDP and the Business Cycle
factors.segmentsHitRaw: Office (follows corporate profits and spending); Retail (follows corporate profits and spending); Hotels (follows corporate profits and spending); Logistics (trade and consumption); Data centres and towers (tech investment); Homebuilding (follows confidence, credit and jobs, and leads the cycle)
factors.whyItMatters: Growth drives jobs, profits and spending, which drive demand for every property type. The cycle also determines why rates move: cuts in a slowdown are very different from cuts after inflation cools. Real estate is cyclical and amplifies the economy's moves because of leverage.

direction.down: Recession hurts demand, but usually brings rate cuts. Boom and overheating end in higher rates and oversupply.

factors.backdrop: The cycle matters most when it turns: from expansion to slowdown (rates high, credit tight) or from recession to recovery (rates falling, credit easing). Real estate usually reacts with a lag, except housing, which often turns first. The best entry point is often late in a slowdown, once cuts begin and before demand recovers.
factors.example: Companies earn less in a downturn and hire fewer people. They rent less office space and cancel expansions. A few quarters later, when the economy recovers and rates are lower, they start hiring and renting again.

watchouts.title: #1 WHO LEADS AND WHO LAGS
watchouts.detail: Housing and homebuilding tend to turn first, because mortgage rates and confidence react quickly. Logistics and retail follow consumer demand. Offices and hotels lag, because companies and travellers cut and restore budgets more slowly. Property values often bottom after the economy does.

watchouts.title: #2 PHASES SUMMARISED
watchouts.detail: Early recovery: rates are low, credit eases, housing rebounds first. -> Expansion: rents and occupancy rise, development starts. -> Late cycle: rates rise, costs climb, new supply arrives, growth slows. -> Recession: vacancy rises, rents fall, defaults rise, rates are cut. -> Your thesis assumes we move from late cycle to early recovery.

watchouts.title: #3 CUTS FOR THE RIGHT OR WRONG REASON
watchouts.detail: A cut because inflation fell is bullish: income stays intact and financing gets cheaper. A cut because the economy is collapsing is less so: tenants struggle to pay and lenders turn cautious, even if rates fall. Morningstar's view of a 2028-29 rebound assumes the first type.

indicators.sources: BEA and Fed (US); Eurostat, ECB and PMIs (Europe).

factors.name: Interest Rates
factors.segmentsHitRaw: Not given as a single list in the notes -- this factor IS the organising variable of the whole thesis, so segmentsHit mirrors the SEED DATA /10 rate-impact ranking across all business-model segments.
factors.whyItMatters: Opens with a typo in the notes: 'The first one and most impactful is definitely real estate...' -- should read 'the most impactful is definitely interest rates'. The actual content explains REITs (debt, valuations/cap rates, shareholder leverage amplification, competition with govt bonds) and homebuilders (mortgage affordability, both-sides margin squeeze, operating leverage) as the two most rate-sensitive business types, ranked 'from most impacted to least impacted'.

reitMechanics.detail: REITs buy properties worth hundreds of millions or billions, often financing part of those purchases with borrowed money. When interest rates rise: refinancing debt becomes more expensive -> interest expenses increase over time -> less cash may be available for shareholders.

Properties are commonly valued by dividing annual net operating income by the return investors require (the capitalization rate, or cap rate). Valuation is implied by the yield INVESTORS DEMAND, which is generally above government bond yields -- which is why the two are very connected.

A REIT has EUR1b of property assets and EUR400m of debt (NAV = EUR600m). If property value falls 10% to EUR900m, debt stays at EUR400m, so NAV falls to EUR500m -- a 16.7% NAV decline from a 10% asset decline. If property value rises 10%, the notes state 'Property Assets: EUR1.05b' -- but 1b + 10% = EUR1.10b, and only EUR1.10b minus EUR400m = EUR700m reproduces the stated +16.7% NAV move (EUR600m -> EUR700m). The EUR1.05b figure is an arithmetic error in the notes.

REIT dividends compete with government bonds. If a REIT offers a 5% dividend yield and government bonds yield 2%, the REIT looks attractive. If government bonds also yield 5%, investors can get a similar yield at lower risk from the bond.

homebuilderMechanics.detail: A buyer wants a EUR400,000 house with a EUR320,000 mortgage over 30 years. At 3%: EUR1,349/month. At 5%: EUR1,718/month. At 7%: EUR2,129/month -- about 58% more per month for the same mortgage when the rate goes from 3% to 7%.
Demand falls: higher mortgage payments mean fewer buyers can afford new houses. Costs rise: construction and land financing become more expensive when debt is repriced.

A homebuilder sells houses for EUR400,000 and spends EUR360,000 building and selling each one -- profit EUR40k. If rates rise and buyers can't afford the same mortgage, the builder cuts price 5% to EUR380,000; profit falls from EUR40k to EUR20k -- a 50% profit decline from a 5% price cut. This is operating leverage: small changes in revenue can produce much larger percentage changes in profit.

EU.situation: 2.50% as of October 2026, up from 2.00% a year ago. The ECB has been raising rates, not cutting them, as inflation picked back up. Markets expect no change at the 29 Oct 2026 meeting (about 93% odds of a hold).

France's 10-year bond yield broke above 5% -- the highest since 2002 -- amid a budget standoff and protests. The gap between French and German bond yields widened sharply to about 1.6 percentage points, matching the notes' claim that this gap is at its widest since the Eurozone crisis. This is the clearest real-world sign that European yields are under real stress, though it's driven by France's own political problems, not a broad European rate move.
